claim: Causal loss-of-function (LOF) variants for Mendelian and severe complex diseases are enriched in 'mutation intolerant' genes.
source: Causal loss-of-function (LOF) variants for Mendelian and severe complex diseases are enriched in 'mutation intolerant' genes.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding in the abstract, supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work.

claim: Estimated fitness costs for the loss of a gene copy are typically above 1%.
source: Estimated fitness costs for the loss of a gene copy are typically above 1%; they tend to be largest for X-linked genes, whether or not they have a Y homolog, followed by autosomal genes and genes in the pseudoautosomal region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the posterior distributions inferred from exome sequences in 56,855 individuals as described in the methods and results.

claim: Fitness costs for the loss of a gene copy tend to be largest for X-linked genes, whether or not they have a Y homolog, followed by autosomal genes and genes in the pseudoautosomal region.
source: Estimated fitness costs for the loss of a gene copy are typically above 1%; they tend to be largest for X-linked genes, whether or not they have a Y homolog, followed by autosomal genes and genes in the pseudoautosomal region.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of inferred fitness effects across different chromosomal compartments as shown in the results.

claim: Probands carry an excess of mutations with estimated fitness effects above 10%.
source: Probands carry an excess of mutations with estimated fitness effects above 10%; as we show by simulation, when sampled in the population, such highly deleterious mutations are typically only a couple of generations old.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of de novo mutations in probands to the DFE of all possible LOF mutations, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: When sampled in the population, highly deleterious mutations (fitness effects above 10%) are typically only a couple of generations old.
source: Probands carry an excess of mutations with estimated fitness effects above 10%; as we show by simulation, when sampled in the population, such highly deleterious mutations are typically only a couple of generations old.
evidence: This is demonstrated through forward simulations showing the age distribution of mutations with different selection coefficients.

claim: The proportion of highly deleterious mutations carried by probands reflects the typical age of onset of the disease.
source: Moreover, the proportion of highly deleterious mutations carried by probands reflects the typical age of onset of the disease.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of DFEs across different diseases with different ages of onset, as shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: A greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in pedigree than case-control studies.
source: The study design also has a discernible influence: a greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in pedigree than case-control studies, and for autism, in simplex than multiplex families and in female versus male probands.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of DFEs from pedigree studies (Figure 4) versus case-control studies (Appendix 1—figure 11).

claim: For autism, a greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in simplex than multiplex families.
source: The study design also has a discernible influence: a greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in pedigree than case-control studies, and for autism, in simplex than multiplex families and in female versus male probands.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of DFEs across different autism cohorts with varying proportions of simplex and multiplex families, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: For autism, a greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in female versus male probands.
source: The study design also has a discernible influence: a greater proportion of highly deleterious mutations is detected in pedigree than case-control studies, and for autism, in simplex than multiplex families and in female versus male probands.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of DFEs between male and female probands in autism cohorts, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Individuals carrying a loss-of-function (LOF) allele that negatively impacts their ability to survive and reproduce will leave fewer descendants on average.
source: All else being equal, individuals carrying a loss-of-function (LOF) allele that negatively impacts their ability to survive and reproduce in their environment will leave fewer descendants on average, and consequently that LOF allele will be at lower frequency in the population at present day.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of population genetics and evolutionary theory.

claim: LOF alleles that negatively impact fitness will be at lower frequency in the population at present day.
source: All else being equal, individuals carrying a loss-of-function (LOF) allele that negatively impacts their ability to survive and reproduce in their environment will leave fewer descendants on average, and consequently that LOF allele will be at lower frequency in the population at present day.
evidence: This follows from the principle of natural selection and is a foundational concept in population genetics.

claim: Observing a depletion of LOF variants in a gene relative to putatively neutral variants is indicative of their deleteriousness.
source: Therefore, observing a depletion of LOF variants in a gene relative to putatively neutral variants is indicative of their deleteriousness.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the principle that deleterious alleles are maintained at lower frequencies due to selection.

claim: pLI relies on the average depletion of observed LOF variants in genes annotated as recessive or severely haploinsufficient in the ClinGen dosage sensitivity gene list and a hand-curated gene set of Mendelian disorders to classify genes as 'neutral,' 'recessive,' or 'haploinsufficient'.
source: pLI relies on the average depletion of observed LOF variants in genes annotated as recessive or severely haploinsufficient in the ClinGen dosage sensitivity gene list and a hand-curated gene set of Mendelian disorders to classify genes as 'neutral,' 'recessive,' or 'haploinsufficient' (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology of pLI as reported in the cited reference.

claim: Genes with a high probability assignment (≥0.9) to the haploinsufficient class are classified as 'extremely loss-of-function intolerant.'
source: Genes with a high probability assignment (≥0.9) to the haploinsufficient class are classified as 'extremely loss-of-function intolerant.'
evidence: This describes the classification criteria used in the pLI measure.

claim: LOEUF does not rely on a reference gene set and is instead a score between 0 and 2, where 0 indicates greater mutation intolerance.
source: LOEUF does not rely on a reference gene set and is instead a score between 0 and 2, where 0 indicates greater mutation intolerance.
evidence: This describes the methodology of LOEUF as reported in the cited reference.

claim: The authors of LOEUF assume a Poisson distribution of LOF mutations in a gene and assign an upper 95% confidence limit on the underlying mean number of such mutations as a factor of the expected number of LOF mutations for this gene.
source: Specifically, the authors assume a Poisson distribution of LOF mutations in a gene and assign an upper 95% confidence limit on the underlying mean number of such mutations as a factor of the expected number of LOF mutations for this gene (Karczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology underlying LOEUF as reported in the cited reference.

claim: Genes classified as highly 'mutation intolerant' by pLI and LOEUF are enriched for variants that lead to Mendelian genetic diseases.
source: Genes classified as highly 'mutation intolerant' by these measures are enriched for variants that lead to Mendelian genetic diseases (e.g., Beck et al., 2020; Chopra et al., 2022; Hansen et al., 2019; Oved et al., 2020; Timberlake et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies showing this enrichment.

claim: A number of recent papers report an enrichment of variants in 'mutation-intolerant genes' for severe complex disease risk.
source: A number of recent papers report an enrichment of variants in 'mutation-intolerant genes' for severe complex disease risk as well (e.g., Antaki et al., 2022; Cappi et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Palmer et al., 2022; Sanders et al., 2019; Satterstrom et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2022; Wilfert et al., 2021; Zoghbi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies showing this enrichment.

claim: pLI and LOEUF are often relied on to classify unknown variants in terms of their likely pathogenic effects.
source: In turn, pLI and LOEUF are often relied on to classify unknown variants in terms of their likely pathogenic effects (e.g., Gudmundsson et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2022; Qi et al., 2021; Sharo et al., 2022; Wang and Li, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies that use these measures for variant classification.

claim: Measures such as pLI and LOEUF implicitly assume an underlying population genetic model of mutation-selection balance.
source: Measures such as pLI and LOEUF implicitly assume an underlying population genetic model of mutation-selection balance (Cassa et al., 2017; Fuller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of these measures in the context of population genetic theory, supported by cited references.

claim: pLI and LOEUF reflect fitness effects over evolutionary time scales, rather than haploinsufficiency with regard to any particular phenotype.
source: Viewing them in light of this model clarifies that they reflect fitness effects over evolutionary time scales, rather than haploinsufficiency with regard to any particular phenotype (Fuller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of these measures in the context of population genetic theory, supported by the cited reference.

claim: For an autosomal gene, pLI and LOEUF are proxies of the fitness reduction in heterozygotes relative to individuals with two intact copies, commonly parameterized as hs in population genetic models.
source: More precisely, for an autosomal gene, they are proxies of the fitness reduction in heterozygotes relative to individuals with two intact copies, commonly parameterized as hs in population genetic models, where s is the fitness cost of losing both copies and h indicates the extent of dominance in fitness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of these measures in the context of population genetic theory.

claim: In a random-mating population with some selection against the loss of one copy, homozygotes should be too infrequent to appreciably affect allele dynamics.
source: Assuming that there is some selection against the loss of one copy, in a random-mating population, homozygotes should be too infrequent to appreciably affect allele dynamics (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010), and the depletion of LOF variants in a gene will be reflective of the strength of selection acting on heterozygotes, hs.
evidence: This is a standard result in population genetics, supported by the cited reference.

claim: The depletion of LOF variants in a gene will be reflective of the strength of selection acting on heterozygotes, hs.
source: Assuming that there is some selection against the loss of one copy, in a random-mating population, homozygotes should be too infrequent to appreciably affect allele dynamics (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010), and the depletion of LOF variants in a gene will be reflective of the strength of selection acting on heterozygotes, hs.
evidence: This follows from the principle that homozygotes are rare when there is selection against heterozygotes.

claim: At most X-linked genes, males are hemizygous and females undergo random X-inactivation.
source: The same general reasoning applies to the X chromosome, but with complications, as at most X-linked genes, males are hemizygous and females undergo random X-inactivation.
evidence: This is a well-established biological fact about X-linked genes.

claim: Given the lack of a second copy in males, the sex-averaged fitness cost of a LOF should be higher on X-linked genes than on autosomes all else being equal.
source: Given the lack of a second copy in males, the sex-averaged fitness cost of a LOF should be higher than on autosomes all else being equal, and X-linked genes are therefore expected to show a greater depletion of LOF variants (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from population genetics, supported by the cited reference.

claim: X-linked genes are expected to show a greater depletion of LOF variants than autosomal genes.
source: Given the lack of a second copy in males, the sex-averaged fitness cost of a LOF should be higher than on autosomes all else being equal, and X-linked genes are therefore expected to show a greater depletion of LOF variants (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from population genetics, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Under a model for mutation and genetic drift, the observed depletion of LOF variants can be used to directly infer the parameter hs.
source: Under a model for mutation and genetic drift, the observed depletion of LOF variants can be used to directly infer the parameter hs; in fact, under a constant population size model and some models of population size changes, and assuming all LOF variants within a gene have the same fitness effect, the sum of the frequencies of LOF variants in a gene is close to a sufficient statistic for hs (see Fuller et al., 2019; Simons et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical result from population genetics, supported by the cited references.

claim: Under a constant population size model and some models of population size changes, and assuming all LOF variants within a gene have the same fitness effect, the sum of the frequencies of LOF variants in a gene is close to a sufficient statistic for hs.
source: Under a model for mutation and genetic drift, the observed depletion of LOF variants can be used to directly infer the parameter hs; in fact, under a constant population size model and some models of population size changes, and assuming all LOF variants within a gene have the same fitness effect, the sum of the frequencies of LOF variants in a gene is close to a sufficient statistic for hs (see Fuller et al., 2019; Simons et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical result from population genetics, supported by the cited references.

claim: A pair of recent studies estimated hs for autosomal genes from ~30,000 individuals, initially under a deterministic approximation and subsequently incorporating a plausible model of demographic history.
source: A pair of recent studies took this approach to estimate hs for autosomal genes from ~30,000 individuals, initially under a deterministic approximation (Cassa et al., 2017), which neglects the effects of genetic drift and changes in population size (Charlesworth and Hill, 2019; Weghorn et al., 2019), and subsequently incorporating a plausible model of demographic history (Weghorn et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes prior work on estimating hs, supported by the cited references.

claim: The deterministic approximation used in Cassa et al., 2017 neglects the effects of genetic drift and changes in population size.
source: A pair of recent studies took this approach to estimate hs for autosomal genes from ~30,000 individuals, initially under a deterministic approximation (Cassa et al., 2017), which neglects the effects of genetic drift and changes in population size (Charlesworth and Hill, 2019; Weghorn et al., 2019), and subsequently incorporating a plausible model of demographic history (Weghorn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a critique of the deterministic approximation, supported by the cited references.

claim: Estimates of hs and proxies like 'measures of intolerance' are reflective of fitness effects over many ancestors and many generations.
source: As these considerations also make clear, however, estimates of hs and proxies like 'measures of intolerance' are reflective of fitness effects over many ancestors, i.e., genetic backgrounds and environments, and many generations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what these estimates represent in an evolutionary context.

claim: Given how drastically the human environment has changed in the recent past, as well as evidence for variable penetrance of disease mutations, it is unclear what relationship to expect between evolutionary fitness costs and present-day disease risk.
source: Given how drastically the human environment has changed in the recent past, as well as evidence for variable penetrance of disease mutations (Cooper et al., 2013; Kingdom et al., 2022), it is unclear what relationship to expect to present-day disease risk.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the relationship between evolutionary fitness and present-day disease risk, supported by cited evidence of variable penetrance.

claim: The study estimated the posterior distributions of hs for the loss of a gene copy on autosomes using exome sequences from 55,855 individuals.
source: To this end, we estimated the posterior distributions of hs for the loss of a gene copy on autosomes using exome sequences from 55,855 individuals.
evidence: This describes the data and methods used in the study.

claim: The study extended the model to different compartments of the X chromosome, taking into account sex differences in mutation and selection, to obtain estimates for X-linked genes.
source: We also extended the model to different compartments of the X chromosome, taking into account sex differences in mutation and selection, to obtain estimates for X-linked genes.
evidence: This describes the methodological extension to the X chromosome.

claim: For each of 18,282 autosomal and X-linked genes, the study estimated the posterior distribution of the fitness cost for heterozygous carriers (hs) of LOF alleles using a sequential Monte Carlo Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC-SMC) approach.
source: For each of 18,282 autosomal and X-linked genes, we estimated the posterior distribution of the fitness cost for heterozygous carriers (hs) of LOF alleles using a sequential Monte Carlo Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC-SMC) approach (Figure 1A; see Supplementary file 2 for these estimates, and analogous ones for the X-chromosome).
evidence: This describes the methods and scope of the analysis.

claim: The study simulated a Wright–Fisher population forward in time to generate the frequency of LOF at a gene and compare it to the frequency observed in the Non-Finnish European (NFE) sample of 55,855 individuals in gnomAD.
source: To this end, we simulated a Wright–Fisher population forward in time in order to generate the frequency of LOF at a gene and compare it to the frequency observed in the Non-Finnish European (NFE) sample of 55,855 individuals in gnomAD (Karczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the simulation approach used in the study.

claim: The study assumed that LOF alleles arise at a mutation rate μ per gene per generation as described in Samocha et al., 2014 and Karczewski et al., 2020.
source: We assumed that LOF alleles arise at a mutation rate μ per gene per generation (as described in Samocha et al., 2014; Karczewski et al., 2020) and that any high-confidence LOF mutation in a gene has the same fitness cost (Agarwal and Przeworski, 2021).
evidence: This describes the assumptions about mutation rates used in the study.

claim: The study assumed that any high-confidence LOF mutation in a gene has the same fitness cost.
source: We assumed that LOF alleles arise at a mutation rate μ per gene per generation (as described in Samocha et al., 2014; Karczewski et al., 2020) and that any high-confidence LOF mutation in a gene has the same fitness cost (Agarwal and Przeworski, 2021).
evidence: This describes a key modeling assumption of the study.

claim: The study assumed a demographic history for the population based on the Schiffels and Durbin, 2014 model, which was modified slightly to better match neutral polymorphism levels observed in the NFE sample.
source: We also assumed a demographic history for the population, based on the Schiffels and Durbin, 2014 model (Schiffels and Durbin, 2014), which we modified slightly to better match neutral polymorphism levels observed in the NFE sample (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the demographic model used in the study.

claim: Among the 17,318 autosomal genes analyzed, the mean maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of hs is 0.058 while the median is 0.018.
source: Among the remaining 17,318 autosomal genes (Figure 1B), the mean maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of hs is 0.058 while the median is 0.018; in other words, the loss of a gene copy typically inflicts a decrease in fitness of greater than 1%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the analysis, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The median constraint under the prior is only 0.04%.
source: The data thus provide evidence of strong constraint for many genes: by contrast, the median constraint under the prior is only 0.04%.
evidence: This is a comparison of the inferred constraint to the prior expectation.

claim: Inferred MAP values of hs span several orders of magnitude, ranging from ~10–6 (GOLGA8S) to 0.55 (RIF1).
source: Inferred MAP values of hs span several orders of magnitude, however, ranging from ~10–6 (GOLGA8S) to 0.55 (RIF1).
evidence: This describes the range of estimated selection coefficients across genes.

claim: There is good agreement between the relative ranks of genes using point estimates of hs and a previous estimate of selection coefficients on LOF alleles (Spearman's rank correlation = 0.82).
source: Overall, there is good agreement between the relative ranks of genes (using our point estimates of hs) and a previous estimate of selection coefficients on LOF alleles (Weghorn et al., 2019) (Spearman's rank correlation = 0.82) (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: The point estimates of hs are somewhat less congruent with previous estimates (R = 0.72).
source: The point estimates themselves are somewhat less congruent (R = 0.72); this is to be expected as the previous approach relied on a smaller sample and the grid of selection coefficients led to a ridge of estimates near hs = 0.4% (see Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, with an explanation for the difference.

claim: Of the 9987 genes for which the point estimate is indicative of strong selection (hs > 10–2), ~35% have at least 5% of their probability mass on quite weak selection (hs < 10–4).
source: Even for genes with large point estimates, there can be substantial probability mass on much weaker selection (e.g., hs < 10–4): for example, of the 9987 genes for which the point estimate is indicative of strong selection (hs > 10–2), ~35% have at least 5% of their probability mass on quite weak selection (hs < 10–4).
evidence: This describes the uncertainty in the estimates.

claim: Based on point estimates alone, it appears that over two-thirds of all autosomal genes in humans are under strong constraint.
source: As a result, whereas based on point estimates alone, it appears that over two-thirds of all autosomal genes in humans are under strong constraint (Figure 1B; Weghorn et al., 2019), based on summing posterior probabilities of hs > 1% for each gene, only half (48%) are estimated to be highly constrained.
evidence: This is a summary of the results, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Based on summing posterior probabilities of hs > 1% for each gene, only half (48%) of autosomal genes are estimated to be highly constrained.
source: As a result, whereas based on point estimates alone, it appears that over two-thirds of all autosomal genes in humans are under strong constraint (Figure 1B; Weghorn et al., 2019), based on summing posterior probabilities of hs > 1% for each gene, only half (48%) are estimated to be highly constrained.
evidence: This is a summary of the results accounting for uncertainty.

claim: The prior likelihood of a gene being highly constrained is 26%.
source: Nonetheless, this number is still much higher than the prior likelihood of a gene being highly constrained (of 26%).
evidence: This is a comparison to the prior expectation.

claim: 73% of genes on the non-PAR X are estimated to be under strong selection (sex-averaged selection on the loss of one copy is above 1%).
source: Consistent with this idea, 73% of genes on the non-PAR X are estimated to be under strong selection (i.e., the sex-averaged selection on the loss of one copy is above 1%), whereas only 48% are for autosomes (Figure 1B and C; see also Appendix 1—figure 8A for a comparison based on point estimates, with p<10–15 by means of a Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a comparison of constraint between X-linked and autosomal genes, shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: X-linked genes show more constraint on average than the 19 genes in the PARs.
source: These X-linked genes also show more constraint on average than the 19 genes in the PARs, which have two expressed copies in both males and females: of the 19 PAR genes, we estimate that only 14% are under strong selection (see also Appendix 1—figure 8A; p=9.9 × 10–9 for a comparison based on point estimates of hs for genes within and outside the PAR on the X).
evidence: This is a comparison of constraint between non-PAR X-linked genes and PAR genes.

claim: Of the 19 PAR genes, only 14% are estimated to be under strong selection.
source: These X-linked genes also show more constraint on average than the 19 genes in the PARs, which have two expressed copies in both males and females: of the 19 PAR genes, we estimate that only 14% are under strong selection (see also Appendix 1—figure 8A; p=9.9 × 10–9 for a comparison based on point estimates of hs for genes within and outside the PAR on the X).
evidence: This is a summary statistic for PAR genes.

claim: 93% of the 16 non-PAR X genes with a Y-chromosome homolog are estimated to be under strong selection.
source: Less expected are our findings for 16 non-PAR X genes with a Y-chromosome homolog (San Roman et al., 2021; see 'Materials and methods'): 93% are estimated to be under strong selection.
evidence: This is a summary statistic for X-linked genes with Y homologs.

claim: The loss of one copy of non-PAR X genes with a Y-chromosome homolog appears to be even more deleterious on average than the rest of the non-PAR X (p=9.2 × 10–4).
source: The loss of one copy of these genes appears to be even more deleterious on average than the rest of the non-PAR X (see also Appendix 1—figure 8A; p=9.2 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of constraint between X-linked genes with and without Y homologs.

claim: The fitness cost of the loss of a gene is higher on X than autosomes whether or not the X-linked gene has a Y chromosome homolog and biallelic expression.
source: Thus, the fitness cost of the loss of a gene is higher on X than autosomes whether or not the X-linked gene has a Y chromosome homolog and biallelic expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings comparing X-linked and autosomal genes.

claim: One interpretation of the higher constraint on X-linked genes with Y homologs is that rather than sex-biased expression and X-inactivation being the source of greater selective constraint, differences in gene dosage may be the consequence of selection for a sex-specific function.
source: As noted by San Roman et al., 2021, and suggested by others (e.g., Park et al., 2010; Slavney et al., 2016), one interpretation may be that rather than sex-biased expression and X-inactivation being the source of greater selective constraint on X-linked genes, differences in gene dosage may be the consequence of selection for a sex-specific function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by cited references.

claim: More than 56% of all possible autosomal LOF mutations have an estimated hs > 1%.
source: The area under the DFE indicates that more than 56% of all possible autosomal LOF mutations have an estimated hs > 1%, while 20% have an hs of 10% or greater (Figure 2A shows the result for all autosomal LOF mutations, and Appendix 1—figure 8B for the X chromosome).
evidence: This is a summary of the DFE for all possible LOF mutations, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 20% of all possible autosomal LOF mutations have an hs of 10% or greater.
source: The area under the DFE indicates that more than 56% of all possible autosomal LOF mutations have an estimated hs > 1%, while 20% have an hs of 10% or greater (Figure 2A shows the result for all autosomal LOF mutations, and Appendix 1—figure 8B for the X chromosome).
evidence: This is a summary of the DFE for all possible LOF mutations, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The DFE of de novo LOF mutations identified in a representative sample of human pedigrees should approximate the inferred DFE of all mutational opportunities, other than those at which mutations lead to embryonic lethality.
source: Therefore, the DFE of de novo LOF mutations identified in a representative sample of human pedigrees should approximate the inferred DFE of all mutational opportunities, other than those at which mutations lead to embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the assumption that DNMs are a random sample of all possible mutations.

claim: In a hospital cohort of newborns not ascertained for any disease, the DFE of DNMs does not differ significantly from the DFE of all possible LOF mutations.
source: In both cohorts, the DFE of DNMs does not differ significantly from the DFE of all possible LOF mutations (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In unaffected siblings in the Simon Simplex autism study, the DFE of DNMs does not differ significantly from the DFE of all possible LOF mutations.
source: In both cohorts, the DFE of DNMs does not differ significantly from the DFE of all possible LOF mutations (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The DFE for LOF mutations seen in spermatogonial stem cells does not differ significantly from the DFE of all possible LOF mutations.
source: The same is observed for the set of LOF mutations seen in spermatogonial stem cells (Moore et al., 2021; Figure 2D); as these mutations are not ascertained on viability of embryos, they should even more faithfully reflect the set of all possible DNMs.
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The contribution of autosomal LOF mutations that are lethal in the embryo or in early development is likely relatively small.
source: Although the numbers of mutations are limited, these results suggest that we can treat our estimated DFE as reflective of all possible LOF mutations. Moreover, these findings suggest that the contribution of autosomal LOF mutations that are lethal in the embryo or in early development is likely relatively small.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the DFE of DNMs in unascertained cohorts matches the DFE of all possible mutations.

claim: Approximately 1 in 1000 de novo mutations in humans lead to an LOF.
source: Available data sets on germline mutations identified in human pedigrees indicate that approximately 1 in 1000 de novo mutations in humans lead to an LOF (this estimate does not include the contribution of embryonic lethal mutations) (Goldmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on data from human pedigrees, supported by the cited reference.

claim: With an average of ~70 DNMs per individual, 1 in ~14 people is born with a DNM that leads to an LOF.
source: With an average of ~70 DNMs per individual (Jónsson et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2012), 1 in ~14 people is therefore born with a DNM that leads to an LOF.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the mutation rate and the number of DNMs per individual, supported by cited references.

claim: Roughly 1 in 71 zygotes carry a highly deleterious de novo loss of a gene through a point mutation (hs > 10%).
source: Our estimates indicate that at least 20% of LOF are associated with hs > 10%, so roughly 1 in 71 zygotes carry a highly deleterious de novo loss of a gene through a point mutation.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the DFE and the rate of de novo LOF mutations.

claim: 6.5% of the point mutation LOFs carried by an individual in the UK Biobank have an estimated fitness cost of hs >10%.
source: Given our coverage criteria and after other filters, we estimate that 6.5% of the point mutation LOFs carried by an individual have an estimated fitness cost of hs >10% (see also Appendix 1—figure 9A).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the UK Biobank analysis.

claim: At least 1 in ~15 humans carries a highly deleterious loss of a gene transmitted by a parent.
source: Thus, at least 1 in ~15 humans carries a highly deleterious loss of a gene transmitted by a parent.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the frequency of highly deleterious LOF variants in the UK Biobank.

claim: Individuals who are not diagnosed with severe diseases can carry highly deleterious de novo and segregating variants.
source: That individuals who are not diagnosed with severe diseases can nonetheless carry highly deleterious de novo and segregating variants indicates either that even such large effect mutations have variable penetrance, or that carriers have a subclinical but substantial reduction in fertility.
evidence: This is an observation from the UK Biobank data.

claim: The observation that individuals without severe disease diagnoses carry highly deleterious variants indicates either that even such large effect mutations have variable penetrance, or that carriers have a subclinical but substantial reduction in fertility.
source: That individuals who are not diagnosed with severe diseases can nonetheless carry highly deleterious de novo and segregating variants indicates either that even such large effect mutations have variable penetrance, or that carriers have a subclinical but substantial reduction in fertility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that unaffected individuals carry highly deleterious variants.

claim: For the set of genes with no LOF variants observed in the UK Biobank sample, mutational opportunities are associated with larger estimated hs values than DNMs.
source: For the set of genes with no LOF variants observed in the UK Biobank sample, mutational opportunities are associated with larger estimated hs values than DNMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The DFE of segregating variants is shifted towards lower values of hs on average compared to the DFE of possible DNMs.
source: In contrast, the DFE of segregating variants is shifted towards lower values of hs on average compared to the DFE of possible DNMs.
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs for segregating variants versus DNMs.

claim: The mean hs is higher at lower allele frequencies: singletons in a sample of ~330K chromosomes approach the DFE of observed DNMs and all possible DNMs.
source: In particular, the mean hs is higher at lower allele frequencies: singletons in a sample of ~330K (i.e., at frequency one in 330K) chromosomes approach the DFE of observed DNMs and all possible DNMs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of segregating variants by allele frequency, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: More weakly selected mutations are removed from the population more slowly on average and are more likely to be seen segregating, at higher frequencies on average, than those under strong selection.
source: These observations follow from first principles since more weakly selected mutations are removed from the population more slowly on average and are more likely to be seen segregating, at higher frequencies on average, than those under strong selection.
evidence: This is a standard result from population genetics theory.

claim: Simulations suggest that if hs = 1%, a mutation sampled in the population at present has persisted for a median of ~60 generations.
source: Accordingly, simulations suggest that if hs = 1%, a mutation sampled in the population at present has persisted for a median of ~60 generations, and if hs = 10%, for a median of only three generations (Figure 3C, Appendix 1—figure 10, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a result from forward simulations, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Simulations suggest that if hs = 10%, a mutation sampled in the population at present has persisted for a median of only three generations.
source: Accordingly, simulations suggest that if hs = 1%, a mutation sampled in the population at present has persisted for a median of ~60 generations, and if hs = 10%, for a median of only three generations (Figure 3C, Appendix 1—figure 10, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a result from forward simulations, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the pedigree studies, there is a clear enrichment for mutations with large values of hs in cases compared to what is expected for a random sample of de novo LOF mutations in the population.
source: In the pedigree studies, there is a clear enrichment for mutations with large values of hs in cases compared to what is expected for a random sample of de novo LOF mutations in the population (Figure 4A–F).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs for disease cohorts versus all possible mutations, shown in Figure 4.

claim: 50% of LOF mutations in the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) cohort have hs >10%.
source: For instance, 50% of LOF mutations in the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) cohort, which consists of individuals with severe developmental disorders, have hs >10%; in comparison, the area under the DFE for a random sample of LOF mutations is only about 20%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the DDD cohort analysis.

claim: A significant enrichment of highly deleterious mutations is observed for developmental disorders, congenital heart disease, developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, autism, and schizophrenia, but not for Tourette's syndrome and OCD.
source: A significant enrichment of highly deleterious mutations is observed for the four other diseases examined, all but Tourette's syndrome and OCD.
evidence: This is a summary of the enrichment analysis across different diseases.

claim: On the X chromosome, there is a similar enrichment of LOF mutations with hs > 10% in the study of developmental disorders.
source: On the X chromosome, there is a similar enrichment of LOF mutations with hs > 10% in the study of developmental disorders (Appendix 1—figure 8C); for other diseases, we do not have sufficient data for the X.
evidence: This is a summary of the enrichment analysis for X-linked genes in developmental disorders.

claim: The mutations that distinguish individuals ascertained for severe disease from a more representative sample are highly deleterious.
source: Thus, the mutations that distinguish individuals ascertained for severe disease from a more representative sample are highly deleterious.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings comparing disease cohorts to population samples.

claim: Highly deleterious mutations identified in disease cohorts do not appear to be fully penetrant in that they are also carried by individuals in the UK Biobank who self-report as healthy.
source: At the same time, such mutations do not appear to be fully penetrant in that they are also carried by individuals in the UK Biobank who self-report as healthy (Appendix 1—figure 9B; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an observation from the UK Biobank analysis.

claim: The degree to which cases are enriched for highly deleterious mutations varies by disease.
source: The degree to which cases are enriched for highly deleterious mutations varies by disease, as can be seen by contrasting the findings for developmental disorders with those for schizophrenia (p<<10–5, 'Materials and methods'), or with Tourette's syndrome and OCD (p<<10–5, 'Materials and methods'), for example.
evidence: This is a comparison of enrichment across different diseases.

claim: Differences in the DFEs across diseases likely reflect, at least in part, the genetic architecture of the disease and how correlated the disease phenotype is to fitness.
source: These differences in the DFEs across diseases likely reflect, at least in part, the genetic architecture of the disease (e.g., how many causal mutations of large effect there are), and, relatedly, how correlated the disease phenotype is to fitness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences in DFEs across diseases.

claim: For more severe diseases, a higher fraction of DNMs are LOF and the LOF mutations identified are more deleterious.
source: Roughly ordering the diseases by their typical age of onset as a proxy of severity, we see that for more severe diseases, a higher fraction of DNMs are LOF and the LOF mutations identified are more deleterious (Figure 4A–F, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of DFEs across diseases ordered by age of onset.

claim: The 2.5-fold enrichment of LOF mutations with hs > 10% due to ascertainment on developmental disorders implies that a DNM identified in a gene with an estimated hs > 10% has a ~60% chance of being causal.
source: The 2.5-fold enrichment of LOF mutations with hs > 10% due to ascertainment on developmental disorders implies that a DNM identified in a gene with an estimated hs > 10% has a ~60% ( = (2.5–1)/2.5) chance of being causal.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the enrichment of highly deleterious mutations in the DDD cohort.

claim: Highly deleterious mutations are more likely to be causal for diseases that are expected to arise in development or early childhood than for those with a typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood.
source: Again roughly ordering the diseases by their average age of onset, highly deleterious mutations are more likely to be causal for diseases that are expected to arise in development or early childhood than for those with a typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood (Figure 4A–F, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of DFEs across diseases ordered by age of onset.

claim: If we consider only genes that have more than one LOF mutation in any of the autism cohorts, there is an almost twofold enrichment of hs > 10% mutations compared to all LOFs seen in autism.
source: Accordingly, if we consider only genes that have more than one LOF mutation in any of the autism cohorts (Figure 4G), there is an almost twofold enrichment of hs > 10% mutations compared to all LOFs seen in autism (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs for recurrently hit genes versus all genes in autism, shown in Figures 4G and 4D.

claim: When more than one de novo LOF mutation has been found in the same gene in small numbers of pedigrees ascertained for a disease, those LOF mutations are more likely to be causal.
source: This observation suggests that, as expected, when more than one de novo LOF mutation has been found in the same gene in small numbers of pedigrees ascertained for a disease, those LOF mutations are more likely to be causal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the enrichment of highly deleterious mutations in recurrently hit genes.

claim: A similarly high enrichment of highly deleterious mutations is seen when conditioning on genes that overlap between autism and schizophrenia cohorts, and autism and developmental disorders.
source: Interestingly, a similarly high enrichment of highly deleterious mutations is seen when conditioning on genes that overlap between autism and schizophrenia cohorts, and autism and developmental disorders (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs for genes shared between different disease cohorts, shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: A gene with two or more independent LOF events in pedigrees ascertained for two different diseases may be more likely to be causal for at least one.
source: The explanation may be similar: a gene with two or more independent LOF events in pedigrees ascertained for two different diseases may be more likely to be causal for at least one.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the enrichment in genes shared between diseases.

claim: An LOF mutation that increases the risk of multiple types of disease or leads to a more severe disease state encompassing multiple syndromes tends to be more severe in its fitness effects.
source: But it may also be that an LOF mutation that increases the risk of multiple types of disease or leads to a more severe disease state encompassing multiple syndromes tends to be more severe in its fitness effects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the enrichment in genes shared between diseases.

claim: In case-control studies of autism, schizophrenia, developmental epilepsy, and bipolar disorder, cases show only a small enrichment of highly deleterious variants over controls.
source: Among such variants, cases show only a small enrichment of highly deleterious variants over controls, which is statistically significant for autism, epilepsy, and schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a summary of the analysis of rare variants in case-control studies.

claim: The small enrichment of highly deleterious variants in case-control studies is expected because a non-negligible fraction of controls harbor highly deleterious alleles.
source: These findings are expected: given that a non-negligible fraction of controls harbor highly deleterious alleles (~6.5% in a relatively healthy cohort; Appendix 1—figure 9A and 11), a large fraction of cases would have to carry such mutations for the enrichment to be appreciable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the small enrichment observed in case-control studies.

claim: Almost all of the mutations compared between cases and controls in case-control studies are inherited rather than de novo, so have lower hs on average.
source: Moreover, almost all of the mutations compared between cases and controls are inherited rather than de novo, so have lower hs on average (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation about the nature of mutations in case-control studies, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: For a given disease, the DFE of the mutations discovered depends on the design of the mapping study.
source: These findings underscore that for a given disease, the DFE of the mutations discovered depends on the design of the mapping study.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings comparing different study designs.

claim: The DFE for de novo LOF mutations in affected males with developmental disorders is very similar to the DFE for mutations seen in affected females.
source: The DFE for de novo LOF mutations in affected males is very similar to the DFE for mutations seen in affected females (Figure 5A and B), and to the DFE for the full sample of 24K trios with developmental disorders (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs by sex in the DDD cohort, shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: For autism, the DFE varies markedly by cohort and by sex.
source: In contrast, for autism, the DFE varies markedly by cohort and by sex (Figures 4D and 5C–J).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs across different autism cohorts and by sex, shown in Figures 4D and 5C-J.

claim: There is a shift of the DFE to smaller hs values among DNMs mapped in multiplex versus simplex families.
source: Consistent with the notion that large effect mutations underlie sporadic cases and a shared oligogenic or polygenic background contributes more to risk in familial cases (e.g., Antaki et al., 2022; Wilfert et al., 2021), there is a shift of the DFE to smaller hs values among DNMs mapped in multiplex versus simplex families (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs between simplex and multiplex families, shown in Figures 5I and 5J.

claim: De novo LOF mutations in simplex cohorts are on average more deleterious than those in cohorts that contain multiplex families.
source: In other words, de novo LOF mutations in simplex cohorts are on average more deleterious than those in cohorts that contain multiplex families.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparison between simplex and multiplex families.

claim: Affected female individuals in Simplex cohorts carry mutations that are much more deleterious than males (p<<10–5).
source: Further, although the vast majority of probands are male, affected female individuals in Simplex cohorts carry mutations that are much more deleterious (p<<10–5, Appendix 1--figure 12; Figure 5C–H).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs by sex in simplex autism cohorts, shown in Figures 5C-H.

claim: A de novo LOF mutation with hs > 10% seen in female cases of simplex autism is on average 1.2–1.5 times more likely to be causal than a similar mutation in males.
source: Indeed, a de novo LOF mutation with hs > 10% seen in female cases of simplex autism is on average 1.2–1.5 times more likely to be causal than a similar mutation in males (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the enrichment of highly deleterious mutations in female versus male probands.

claim: The finding that affected females in simplex autism cohorts carry more deleterious mutations is consistent with a 'female protective effect' in autism.
source: This finding is consistent with a 'female protective effect' in autism (Jacquemont et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2013; Satterstrom et al., 2020; Wigdor et al., 2022), for instance, if compensation through socialization leads to sporadic autism diagnoses only in females with very severe disease; alternatively, it may reflect a physiological difference in how the disease develops in the two sexes, e.g., through differential effects of sex hormones in development (Ferri et al., 2018; Werling, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sex difference in DFEs, supported by cited references.

claim: A sex difference in DNMs is not detected in multiplex families for autism.
source: Intriguingly, a sex difference in DNMs is not detected in multiplex families (Figure 5I-J), potentially because the disease risk tends to be polygenic in both sexes in such families; in principle, it could also result from females being diagnosed at lower severity thresholds as affected siblings of male probands.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of DFEs by sex in multiplex families, shown in Figures 5I and 5J.

claim: For schizophrenia studies, there is almost no discernible difference between males and females in the DFE.
source: For schizophrenia studies, in turn, there is almost no discernible difference between males and females (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs by sex in schizophrenia cohorts.

claim: For schizophrenia, cases that have a documented family history of mental illness show a shift towards less deleterious DNMs compared to cases without one.
source: While we lack information on simplex and multiplex families, cases that have a documented family history of mental illness show a shift towards less deleterious DNMs compared to cases without one (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: This is a comparison of DFEs by family history in schizophrenia cohorts.

claim: Commonly varying characteristics of individual cohorts influence the severity of variants discovered for a given disease.
source: As with studies of autism, these findings highlight that for a given disease, commonly varying characteristics of individual cohorts influence the severity of variants discovered.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on how study design affects the DFE.

claim: The characteristics of cohorts impact the utility of discovered variants in elucidating the pathophysiology of the disease.
source: Accordingly, these characteristics impact their utility in elucidating the pathophysiology of the disease.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of study design on understanding disease mechanisms.

claim: 285 genes have observed LOF frequencies that are unusually high under a neutral model.
source: Of the genes considered, a subset (285; Supplementary file 1) have observed LOF frequencies that are unusually high under a neutral model (and a fortiori, a model with hs > 0).
evidence: This is a summary of genes excluded from the analysis due to model misspecification.

claim: Genes with unusually high LOF frequencies likely represent cases where the model is misspecified, perhaps because the mutation rate to LOF alleles is in fact higher or due to other biological features.
source: These likely represent cases where our model is misspecified, perhaps because the mutation rate to LOF alleles is in fact higher or due to other biological features (e.g., there is balancing selection on mutations in the gene; see Amorim et al., 2017; Lenz et al., 2016; Monroe et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of why some genes have unusually high LOF frequencies, supported by cited references.

claim: Another possibility for unusually high LOF frequencies is that some mutations are incorrectly annotated as LOF.
source: Another possibility is that some mutations are incorrectly annotated as LOF (Cummings et al., 2020; Karczewski et al., 2020; MacArthur et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a possible explanation for unusually high LOF frequencies, supported by cited references.
